name: Ivan Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, which is independent of AI firms, employers, unions and government. Your answers are confidential. What happens on an ordinary workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 27, with a master’s degree and a chartered accountancy qualification, and lead the tax-return queue at an accounting firm. I spend mornings on account reviews and afternoons ringing clients, including a bakery owner who brings receipts in a shoebox. I use our approved AI receipt sorter every day, then check its flags against bank statements.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things for you outside the office?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner and we have no children. I am paid well for this job, have about nine months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of similar jobs nearby. I usually try new tools early, but I want proof they do not hide tax errors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team a little routine automation gives us room to call clients earlier. The shoebox of receipts from the bakery still needs someone to ask why the totals changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I earn well for this job and have about nine months of expenses saved. A small software shortcut will not threaten my hours, and there are several other firms nearby if ours mismanages it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep using the AI receipt sorter I use each day and compare its flags with the bakery bank statements. In the first year I would keep leading the tax-return review queue and show the partner a monthly count of corrections.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about both pay and the work I enjoy. I would be annoyed if our firm called a time saving a reason to skip a real check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the sorter miss on the bakery file?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It marked a new oven deposit as a normal expense, which changed the tax total. I rang the baker before I let the junior reviewer close the file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend the time saved on another client?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after the current files are checked. I would put the spare hour into questions for clients rather than fill it with more unchecked drafts.

say: I would use small **time savings** to call clients sooner about missing records.
I would keep a **real review** on every tax return.
think: My **high pay** and nine-month cushion make this a secure picture for me.
I can find work at **nearby firms** if my own firm handles changes badly.
do: Keep using my **daily receipt sorter** and compare flags against bank statements.
Lead the **tax review queue** and show partners monthly correction counts.
feel: I feel **calm** about my pay and the routine I enjoy.
S0.quote: The shoebox of receipts from the bakery still needs someone to ask why the totals changed.
fieldNote: His **bakery example** grounds his confidence: he found an oven deposit misclassified and called the client before filing.
He has **nine months saved** and nearby employers, so routine automation feels more like a service improvement than an income threat.

steps.text: Keep sorting bakery receipts and checking flags against bank statements

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the partners to measure errors and client time, not just the number of drafts software finishes. A smaller junior team might save salary now and cost us judgment later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI could take much of the tax writing and account checking I do, so a senior title alone is no shield. My savings and the many firms nearby give me a real choice if our work becomes only clicking approve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the manager to let me pilot the approved drafting system on ten complex returns, recording corrections and client questions. In the first year I would seek a paid advisory vacancy here with written salary and client hours; if no post opens, I would apply to advertised senior roles nearby while staying on payroll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the profession but fairly steady about my own next year. I have enough runway to reject a bad offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a bad advisory offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A title with no client hours and lower pay would be a pay cut dressed as progress. I would ask the manager to put the actual hours and salary in the offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ten returns?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten gives me different client types without risking the whole queue. I can compare the first draft with my working papers and discuss the error list with the juniors.

say: I would ask partners to count **errors and client time**, not just software drafts.
I would warn that losing **junior training** can weaken future reviews.
think: My **tax writing** may shrink, regardless of my senior title.
Nine months saved and **many local firms** let me refuse a poor offer.
do: Pilot **ten complex returns** with manager approval and record corrections.
Seek a **paid advisory vacancy** with written salary and client hours, or apply to advertised local roles while employed.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about the profession but secure in the near term.
S1.quote: A title with no client hours and lower pay would be a pay cut dressed as progress.
fieldNote: He tests **ten varied returns** against working papers, making his daily AI use disciplined rather than uncritical.
His **strong savings** and local options make him willing to reject an advisory title without written pay and client hours.

steps.text: Pilot approved drafting system on ten complex returns if manager permits
Seek written-pay advisory vacancy with client hours; otherwise apply to posted local roles while employed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the firm AGI by 2028 reaches our accounts and tax screens as soon as it arrives. The robots around 2031 are no reason to delay a staffing plan for desk work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of my written review work to vanish once a cheaper system can think as well as I can. Nine months of expenses buys me time, but it does not make my current high salary easy to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would request a written hours forecast and ask to spend one paid day a week observing client tax disputes to learn the hearing work, if the partner agrees. In the first year after 2028, if account-review hours fall, I would apply for a paid dispute vacancy with written salary and hours; if there is none, I would apply to advertised local firms while keeping any remaining paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing a good income, though I am not out of options. I can act before the account balance gets low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start a practice yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on a guess that clients will still pay for my judgment. I would first count the disputes where a person actually helped and compare that with the cost of office space.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your team on the day hours are cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the written notice and ask each person which paid vacancies they want to pursue. I would not promise the robots give accountants another three years.

say: I would say **AGI by 2028** reaches tax desks before capable robots arrive.
I would demand a **written hours forecast** from the firm.
think: I expect most **written review work** to disappear after 2028.
My **nine-month cushion** buys time, but replacing high pay may be hard.
do: Seek partner approval to **observe tax disputes** for one paid day weekly.
After 2028, apply for a **paid dispute vacancy** with written terms if reviews shrink.
Apply to **advertised local firms** while keeping remaining paid hours if no internal vacancy exists.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing high pay, with enough savings to act.
S2.quote: Nine months of expenses buys me time, but it does not make my current high salary easy to replace.
fieldNote: His **income risk** is large despite a strong cushion because the high salary may not follow him into a new role.
He makes **client dispute work** a test with partner-approved paid time, and keeps existing paid hours during any external search.

steps.text: Learn tax disputes one paid day weekly if partner approves
Apply for paid internal dispute vacancy with written salary and hours after 2028 review cuts
Apply to advertised local firms after 2028 if no internal vacancy, keeping paid hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2031 gives the firm time to build a paid client-advice service and tell staff where they fit. Robots arriving around 2034 do not change when our screen work is exposed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years should let me learn whether the tax dispute work can support my wage and add to my savings. I still expect software to take much of the accounts review by 2031, so a nice pilot is not enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask to lead two client dispute meetings each quarter with the partner present to learn the work, if those hours are paid. I would set aside 200 a month while my current salary holds; in the first year after 2031 I would take an advisory opening only with written pay and hours at least equal to my present job, otherwise apply to advertised nearby firms before resigning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy but able to plan. Five years lets me see invoices for actual client advice, not just a slide about a future service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What will you count from those meetings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would record whether the client bought advice and what changed in the tax case. If nobody pays for the work, I would stop calling it a career path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend your savings on a new firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after a year of paid demand and a separate six-month personal reserve. I would not put the rent cushion into office furniture.

say: I would ask for a **paid advice service** with clear staff roles before 2031.
I would remind colleagues the **2034 robots** do not postpone tax desk exposure.
think: I may replace review hours with **paid dispute work**, but only if clients buy it.
I expect much of **accounts review** to move to software in 2031.
do: Lead **two dispute meetings** quarterly with partner approval and paid hours.
Save **200 monthly** while my high salary holds.
Take **advisory work** after 2031 only with matching written pay and hours; otherwise apply nearby while employed.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, with time to test whether clients pay for advice.
S3.quote: I would not put the rent cushion into office furniture.
fieldNote: He wants **paid client invoices** before treating dispute work as a real replacement for account review.
His **200 monthly** transfer depends on current pay, and his later move requires written salary and hours no worse than today.

steps.text: Learn dispute work in two paid quarterly meetings with partner approval
Save 200 monthly while current high salary holds
Take advisory role after 2031 with matching written pay and hours or apply nearby while employed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2036 gives me a decade to build clients who pay for a person to explain complex tax choices. The firm should keep training juniors, because they cannot become advisers without early cases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be running a client practice by 2036, but I know almost any thinking task can still be done by AGI then. The robots in 2039 may affect other work; my desk deadline is earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the partners for a written plan to lead a small tax-dispute desk and keep serving my current clients while we test demand. I would add 250 a month to savings if my high pay holds; in the first year after 2036 I would keep a paid client-advice post if written hours and salary match my present job, or take an advertised senior vacancy nearby before leaving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the next few years because I have pay, assets and several local options. I still want a plan that earns its own keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know the new desk works?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count paid cases each quarter and compare them with the cost of staff hours. A tax-dispute desk with a clever name and no invoices is not a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the partners refuse the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my existing clients and take the same figures to an interview at another local firm with a posted vacancy. I would not quit before an offer with written pay arrives.

say: I would propose a **paid tax-dispute desk** with junior training built in.
I would ask the firm to measure **client invoices** before expanding it.
think: AGI can still take nearly all **thinking tasks** by 2036.
My **high pay and savings** give me time to build paid client relationships.
do: Ask partners for a **written dispute-desk plan** while keeping existing clients.
Save **250 monthly** if high pay holds.
Keep **paid advice work** after 2036 with matching written hours and salary, or take an advertised senior vacancy before leaving.
feel: I feel **calm** about the near term while taking the 2036 change seriously.
S4.quote: A tax-dispute desk with a clever name and no invoices is not a business.
fieldNote: His **long runway** plan has a business test: quarterly paid cases must justify the cost of staff hours.
He has **strong bargaining room** but still requires a written plan and pay terms before changing firms or roles.

steps.text: Keep serving current clients while requesting written dispute-desk plan
Save 250 monthly if current high pay holds
Keep paid advice post after 2036 only with written hours and salary matching current job
Take advertised local senior vacancy before leaving, with a written pay offer

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a strong salary can disappear faster than I can replace it. A written forecast, paid time to test dispute work and real vacancies would help me decide.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who trains the next person to spot a bad bakery expense. An accountant does not learn judgment by approving a finished screen.

headlineQuote: An accountant does not learn judgment by approving a finished screen.
portrait: At **27**, Ivan leads tax reviews with a master’s degree, chartered qualification and daily use of an approved AI receipt sorter.
He earns **high pay**, has nine months saved and can consider many nearby accounting firms.
His **pragmatic approach** tests client dispute demand against paid invoices and written terms before changing roles.
The **2028 change** threatens his high salary; longer runways let him build a paid advice practice and conditional savings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase much of his well-paid review work before a comparable role is ready.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a **written hours forecast**, paid time to test dispute work and actual vacancies.
